Record date: 2130-02-10
South Elizabeth Seychelles Hospital INTERNAL MEDICINE DEPARTMENT Location: 4923 Olivia Parkway Suite 217, Lake Jennabury
PATIENT: Lysander Fairfax Phone: 28451903 email:bradleymorgan@example.org DATE OF BIRTH: 1947-05-12 AGE: 80 years
FOLLOW-UP DATE: 02/10/30 FOLLOWED BY: Dr. Emily Carter
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Persistent shortness of breath and worsening cough with increased sputum production.
HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Mr. Lysander Fairfax returns for a follow-up visit after two days of intensified treatment. He reports continued shortness of breath, now exacerbated to the point of requiring assistance with daily activities. The sputum remains thick, yellow-green, and increased in volume, with the patient noting that he is now producing approximately 100 mL of sputum per day. He describes a persistent cough that is more frequent and disruptive to his sleep, contributing to a heightened sense of anxiety regarding his condition.
The patient continues to experience intermittent low-grade fevers, with temperatures fluctuating between 99F and 100.5F. He denies any chest pain or hemoptysis but expresses concern over his increasing fatigue and difficulty in maintaining adequate oxygen saturation levels, despite the ongoing supplemental oxygen therapy.
REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
General - + significant fatigue, - night sweats, - chills, + intermittent low-grade fever. Pulmonary - + productive cough with thick yellow-green sputum, + increased dyspnea, + wheezing, - hemoptysis. Cardiac - no chest pain, - orthopnea, - paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Gastrointestinal - + mild epigastric discomfort, - stable heartburn, - no nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Musculoskeletal - no joint pain. Neurological - no dizziness or headaches.
PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: - Blood Pressure: 128/80 mmHg - Heart Rate: 94 bpm - Respiratory Rate: 32 breaths/min - Oxygen Saturation: 72% on supplemental oxygen (30 L via nasal cannula).
General: The patient appears markedly fatigued and is in significant respiratory distress, requiring assistance with positioning.
HEENT: No nasal flaring; oropharynx clear, no signs of dehydration.
Lungs: Severe wheezing and prolonged expiration noted on auscultation; bilateral diminished breath sounds; rhonchi and crackles are markedly pronounced, particularly in the lower lung fields.
Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs or gallops; peripheral pulses intact.
Abdomen: Soft, non-tender; mild epigastric discomfort persists; no hepatosplenomegaly.
ASSESSMENT
1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation with ongoing bacterial infection, likely persistent Pseudomonas aeruginosa; sputum characteristics remain concerning for inadequate response to Meropenem. 2. Significant respiratory distress with inadequate improvement despite aggressive antibiotic therapy; persistent bronchial obstruction or secondary infection remains a concern. 3. Increased fatigue and anxiety significantly impacting quality of life; gastrointestinal symptoms remain stable.
PLAN
1. Continue Meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours; review sputum culture results to assess for antibiotic susceptibility and adjust therapy accordingly. 2. Maintain Prednisone at 80 mg daily to control inflammation; tapering plan contingent upon clinical response; continue Omeprazole at 40 mg daily to prevent gastrointestinal complications. 3. Increase supplemental oxygen to 35 L via nasal cannula; consider non-invasive ventilation if oxygen saturation does not improve. 4. Order a repeat chest X-ray to evaluate for any new complications, such as pneumonia or pleural effusion; bronchoscopy is recommended for further evaluation given the lack of improvement. 5. Continue nebulized bronchodilator therapy (Albuterol) every four hours as needed, and maintain Ipratropium bromide therapy; initiate N-acetylcysteine as a mucolytic agent to assist with sputum clearance. 6. Schedule follow-up visit in 24 hours to reassess respiratory function, sputum characteristics, and overall clinical condition; consider immediate referral to pulmonology if no significant improvement is observed.
DISPOSITION
Mr. Fairfax will remain under close observation in the internal medicine unit. The treatment team will continue to monitor his clinical status, particularly focusing on respiratory function and infection management. Patient education will be reinforced regarding the importance of adherence to the treatment regimen and the need to report any new or worsening symptoms, particularly related to respiratory function or changes in sputum production.
